title: Grape Leaf Spot Complex (Mycosphaerella/Septoria complex, Phaeoacremonium, Pseudocercospora vitis)
content: Grape leaf spot and leaf blight is a complex of foliar necrotrophic pathogens causing premature defoliation of wine, table, and juice grapes (Vitis vinifera, V. labrusca, V. aestivalis hybrids) in warm, humid grape-growing regions worldwide including the eastern and midwestern United States, Brazil, Argentina, Uruguay, southern Europe, India, China, Japan, and eastern Australia. The primary components of the leaf spot complex on grapes are: (1) Pseudocercospora vitis (Lev.) Speg. [syn. Cercospora viticola (Ces.) Sacc., teleomorph Mycosphaerella personata; Mycosphaerellaceae, Capnodiales, Dothideomycetes - causes 'Cercospora leaf spot', the most widespread and economically important leaf spot of grapes globally]; (2) Septoria ampelina Berk. & M.A. Curtis (teleomorph Mycosphaerella angulata; causes angular leaf spot / Septoria leaf spot of grapes); (3) Phaeoacremonium aleophilum and Phaeomoniella chlamydospora (secondary foliar symptoms associated with the vascular 'Petri disease' / 'esca complex' on young vines); and (4) Alternaria alternata, Epicoccum nigrum, and Stemphylium vesicarium as secondary saprotrophic invaders of senescent or previously damaged leaf tissue. While individual leaf spot pathogens cause only minor necrotic lesions, the cumulative effect of multiple species attacking the same leaves causes 20-60% premature defoliation in late summer, reducing fruit sugar and anthocyanin accumulation, increasing fruit sunscald, and weakening vine cold hardiness and bud fruitfulness for the subsequent growing season. Symptoms of Pseudocercospora vitis Cercospora leaf spot first appear on the oldest (basal) lower-canopy leaves in early- to mid-summer (4-6 weeks after bloom) as small (1-3 mm), circular to slightly irregular, necrotic tan lesions with a dark brown margin and a narrow chlorotic yellow halo visible when the leaf is held against transmitted light. A close examination with a 10x hand lens reveals a characteristic gray-to-olivaceous velvety tuft of fasciculate conidiophores and obclavate multi-septate Cercospora conidia emerging through stomata on the lower (abaxial) leaf surface in lesion centers. As lesions expand to 5-15 mm, they often become angular (limited by secondary veins) and develop a white ashen center; heavily infected leaves develop 20-80 lesions per blade, turn bright yellow (chlorotic), abscise, and fall prematurely beginning 6-8 weeks before normal harvest. Septoria ampelina angular leaf spot lesions are smaller (1-4 mm), distinctly angular (vein-limited), dark brown to black, and contain small, embedded, black ostiolate pycnidia within the lesion center visible with a 20x dissecting scope. Vines affected by the Phaeoacremonium/Phaeomoniella esca/Petri complex exhibit characteristic 'tiger stripe' interveinal chlorotic and necrotic striping on upper canopy leaves in mid-summer. All members of the grape leaf spot complex overwinter as pseudothecia (sexual Mycosphaerella teleomorph fruiting bodies), pycnidia, and stromatic mycelium on infected fallen grape leaves on the vine floor, in old cane bark crevices, and on wild Vitis and Parthenocissus (Virginia creeper) wild host species. In spring, mature ascospores are forcibly discharged from pseudothecia following rain events and are wind-dispersed onto newly expanding grape leaves; conidia are splash-dispersed from pycnidia during rain showers. Multiple repeated secondary cycles occur throughout the growing season under conditions of high RH (> 85%), temperatures 22-30 C, and 4-8 hours of leaf wetness from rain, dew, or overhead sprinkler irrigation. Because the pathogens require living leaf tissue to penetrate but then switch to necrotrophic nutrition, extended periods of leaf wetness during warm weather, dense shaded canopies, excessive succulent shoot growth from high nitrogen fertilization, and stressed vines with poor root health are all predisposing factors for severe leaf spot epidemics. Management: (1) cultural practices: fall removal of leaf litter from the vine floor by raking, flail mowing and shallow disking to bury infected leaves, or vacuuming in organic systems reduces primary inoculum levels by 40-70% the following spring; maintain open, well-ventilated canopies via appropriate trellising (VSP, GDC, Scott-Henry), shoot thinning, leaf removal in the fruit zone and basal canopy, and shoot positioning to maximize air movement and reduce leaf wetness duration; avoid excessive nitrogen application which promotes late-season succulent shoot growth highly susceptible to Cercospora; ensure adequate potassium fertilization because low vine K status increases susceptibility to Pseudocercospora and Septoria leaf spots. (2) genetic resistance: Vitis vinifera wine grape cultivars vary widely in susceptibility; 'Cabernet Sauvignon', 'Merlot', 'Riesling', 'Pinot Gris' are highly susceptible, while 'Sangiovese', 'Nebbiolo', 'Barbera', 'Syrah', 'Gewurztraminer' show moderate quantitative partial resistance; native American species and their interspecific hybrids (V. labrusca 'Concord', 'Niagara', Catawba; French-American hybrids Vignoles, Chambourcin, Noiret, Corot noir) carry higher levels of polygenic resistance. (3) fungicide programs: because leaf spot complex pathogens are members of the Dothideomycetes (Cercospora/Septoria/Mycosphaerella), standard fungicide programs targeting grape powdery mildew (PM) and black rot (BR) generally provide incidental suppression of leaf spot complex as well; however, in high-pressure years, specific additional sprays may be needed targeting the basal canopy from fruit set through veraison. Most effective fungicide groups in Penn State / APS trials: FRAC 3 DMI triazoles (tebuconazole, difenoconazole, myclobutanil, prothioconazole, tetraconazole, metconazole - excellent protectant + curative activity against Cercospora and Septoria); FRAC 11 QoI (azoxystrobin, pyraclostrobin, trifloxystrobin, fluoxastrobin - good protectant; must be alternated with non-QoI groups to prevent QoI resistance); FRAC 7 SDHI (fluxapyroxad, boscalid, penthiopyrad, benzovindiflupyr, pydiflumetofen, isofetamid - excellent broad-spectrum protectant against leaf spot complex; tank-mix with multi-site); FRAC 9+12 anilino-pyrimidines (cyprodinil, pyrimethanil - moderate control); FRAC M3 multi-site (mancozeb, maneb, metiram, ziram) and FRAC M1 copper (Bordeaux mixture, copper hydroxide) provide solid multi-site protectant control with no resistance risk. Organic production relies on copper (Bordeaux mixture), elemental sulfur (moderate), potassium bicarbonate, Reynoutria sachalinensis extract, and Bacillus amyloliquefaciens QST 713 rotations on a 7-10 day schedule from fruit set through veraison.
